facts.statement: The genus Brachychampsa was first described by Charles W. Gilmore in 1911.
Brachychampsa is an extinct genus of alligatorid that may represent a basal caiman.
facts.quote: Brachychampsa is an extinct genus of alligatorid, possibly a basal caiman.

facts.statement: Brachychampsa lived from the late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous to the late Maastrichtian stage of the Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The genus first appeared during the late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous (Judithian North American stage) and became extinct during the late Maastrichtian stage of the Cretaceous (Lancian North American Land Mammal "Age").

facts.statement: Fossils of Brachychampsa have been reported from New Mexico, Colorado, Wyoming, Montana, North and South Dakota, New Jersey, and Saskatchewan, with confirmed material from Montana, Utah, and New Mexico.
facts.quote: Specimens have been reported from New Mexico, Colorado, Wyoming, Montana, North and South Dakota, New Jersey, and Saskatchewan, though only those from Montana, Utah, and New Mexico are based on material sufficient to justify the referral.

facts.statement: The type species B. montana was first discovered in the Hell Creek Formation of Montana and described by Charles W. Gilmore in 1911.
facts.quote: The type species of Brachychampsa is B. montana, first discovered from the Hell Creek Formation of Montana and described by Charles W. Gilmore in a paper in 1911.

facts.statement: Walter et al. (2022) recovered Brachychampsa as one of the basalmost alligatorines, suggesting definitive stem-group caimans appeared in the earliest Paleocene.
facts.quote: However, Walter et al. (2022) recovered Brachychampsa, Stangerochampsa and Albertochampsa as the basalmost alligatorines based on phylogenetic analysis and claimed that the earliest definitive stem-group caimans are known from the earliest Paleocene.

facts.statement: Sullivan and Lucas (2003) suggested that if Brachychampsa hunted turtles, it likely targeted juveniles or smaller species because most late Cretaceous turtles were too large.
facts.quote: In 2003, Robert M. Sullivan and Spencer G. Lucas observed that most late Cretaceous turtles were probably too big for consumption, and that if they did represent a large portion of Brachychampsa's diet, it would have had to hunt either juveniles or smaller turtle species.

facts.statement: Brachychampsa appeared at the end of the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous and went extinct at the beginning of the Danian stage of the Paleocene, a few million years after the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction.
facts.quote: El género apareció primero a fines de la época del Campaniense del Cretácico Superior (piso geológico Juditiano de Norteamérica) y se extinguió a principios del Daniense en el período Paleoceno (época del Puercano), unos cuantos millones de años después de la Extinción masiva del Cretácico-Terciario.

facts.statement: Brachychampsa is distinguished by an elongated fourth maxillary tooth in the upper jaw.
facts.quote: Brachychampsa se distingue por el alargado cuarto diente maxilar en la mandíbula superior.

facts.statement: Brachychampsa was initially placed in Alligatoridae, then Alligatorinae in 1964, and later placed outside both Alligatorinae and Alligatoridae but within Alligatoroidea in 1994.
facts.quote: Al principio fue situado en la familia moderna Alligatoridae, y luego incluido en la subfamilia Alligatorinae en 1964, solo para ser más tarde colocado afuera tanto de Alligatorinae como de Alligatoridae (pero aún dentro de Alligatoroidea) en 1994.

facts.statement: The time range for Brachychampsa is estimated from 93.9 to 63.4 million years ago, spanning the Turonian to Danian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Turonian to Danian (93.9 to 63.4 million years ago)
